items.new: According to the invariable custom of the fishery, the whale-boat pushes off from the ship with the headsman, or whale-killer, as temporary steersman, and the harpooner, or whale-fastener, pulling the foremost oar, the one known as the harpooner-oar. Now it takes a strong, nervy arm to strike the first iron into the fish; for often, in what is called a long dart, the heavy implement has to be flung a distance of twenty or thirty feet. But however long and exhausting the chase, the harpooner is expected to pull his oar to the utmost all the while; indeed, he is expected to set the rest an example of superhuman activity, not only by incredible rowing, but by repeated loud and fearless shouts; and what it is to keep shouting at the top of your voice while every other muscle is strained and half wrenched out of place — that no one knows but those who have tried it. For my part, I cannot bawl very heartily and work very recklessly at one and the same time. In this straining, bawling state, then, with his back to the fish, the exhausted harpooner all at once hears the exciting cry — "Stand up, and give it to him!" He now has to drop and secure his oar, turn halfway round on his center, seize his harpoon from the crotch, and with what little strength may remain, try to pitch it somehow into the whale. No wonder, taking the whole fleet of whalemen together, that out of fifty fair chances for a dart, not five are successful; no wonder that so many luckless harpooners are madly cursed and demoted; no wonder that some of them actually burst their blood-vessels in the boat; no wonder that some sperm whalemen are gone four years with four barrels; no wonder that to many shipowners whaling is nothing but a losing business; for it is the harpooner who makes the voyage, and if you take the breath out of his body, how can you expect to find it there when it is most wanted!

items.new: *A little item may as well be told here. The strongest and most reliable hold the ship has on the whale when moored alongside is by the flukes, or tail; and since that part, from its greater density, is relatively heavier than any other (except the side-fins), its flexibility, even in death, makes it sink low beneath the surface, so that you cannot reach it by hand from the boat to put the chain around it. But this difficulty is ingeniously overcome: a small, strong line is prepared with a wooden float at its outer end and a weight in its middle, while the other end is made fast to the ship. By skillful management the wooden float is made to rise on the other side of the mass, so that, the line having now girdled the whale, the chain is easily made to follow; and being slipped along the body, it is at last locked fast around the smallest part of the tail, where it joins the broad flukes or lobes.

They viciously snapped not only at each other's spilled entrails, but, bending round like flexible bows, bit at their own; until those entrails seemed swallowed over and over again by the same mouth, only to be voided out the opposite way through the gaping wound. Nor was this all. It was unsafe to meddle with the corpses and ghosts of these creatures. A sort of generic or Pantheistic vitality seemed to lurk in their very joints and bones after what might be called the individual life had departed. One of these sharks, killed and hoisted on deck for the sake of his skin, almost took poor Queequeg's hand off when he tried to shut down the dead lid of its murderous jaw.

items.reason: Invented 'Sometimes a very practiced hand will keep the blade sharp enough to shave off the thin surface of the body without drawing blood'. Lost: 'In its socket, a stiff pole, from twenty to thirty feet long, is inserted for a handle.' Footnote '*' dropped.
items.new: *The whaling-spade used for cutting-in is made of the very best steel; it is about the size of a man's spread hand, and in general shape corresponds to the garden tool it is named after, except that its sides are perfectly flat and its upper end considerably narrower than the lower. This weapon is always kept as sharp as possible, and when in use it is honed now and then, just like a razor. A stiff pole, from twenty to thirty feet long, is fitted into its socket as a handle.

items.reason: Period narration 'said the savage' softened to 'said the harpooner' (brief rule 4; edition keeps 'the savage' elsewhere). Queequeg's speech otherwise kept as the candidate has it.
items.new: "Queequeg no care what god made him shark," said the savage, agonizingly lifting his hand up and down. "Whether Fiji god or Nantucket god — but the god that made shark must be one damn Indian."
